texts.x: UPSC Syllabus: Gs Paper 2- Science and Technology Introduction Global AI investment has centred on advanced models, chips and data centres, encouraging the belief that gains will go to the companies building them. However, the World Bank Group’s World Development Report 2026: The Promise of Artificial Intelligence argues that development gains depend on applying AI…

points: Global AI investment has largely concentrated on advanced models, chips, and data centres, but development gains rely on applying AI to practical problems at scale.
Only 4.5 percent of jobs in low- and middle-income countries are highly exposed to generative AI automation, presenting a lower risk of job displacement.
Another 16.2 percent of jobs in developing nations can experience meaningful productivity gains, as AI complements human labour and expands expertise access.
India has demonstrated strong technology deployment in agriculture, healthcare, and weather forecasting, such as increased sugarcane yields in Baramati and better TB detection.
Challenges include the concentration of AI resources among a few firms, dependence on major providers, inadequate physical infrastructure, and shortages of local-language data.
Gaps in digital skills, limited institutional capacity, and difficulty in scaling successful pilots further hinder widespread and effective AI adoption.
India’s Digital Public Infrastructure, such as Aadhaar and UPI, provides an open-architecture model that supports competition and lowers costs for technology adoption.
The IndiaAI Mission addresses compute capacity, indigenous foundation models via AIKosh, startup financing, and safe AI governance to strengthen domestic capabilities.
Recommendations for India include adapting AI to local needs, adopting a full-stack approach, testing through evidence, strengthening public institutions, and ensuring inclusive growth.
sum.text:
Global AI investment has centred on advanced models, chips and data centres, encouraging the belief that gains will go to the companies building them. However, the World Bank Group’s World Development Report 2026: The Promise of Artificial Intelligence argues that development gains depend on applying AI to practical problems at scale. For India, the challenge is to adapt AI to local needs and spread its benefits widely.
Productivity and Economic Growth: AI can sustain economic growth by improving productivity, expanding access to expertise and making public services more effective.
Lower Risk of Job Automation: Only 4.5% of jobs in low- and middle-income countries are highly exposed to generative AI automation, compared with 14.2% in high-income countries.
Potential for Worker Productivity: Another 16.2% of jobs in low- and middle-income countries could experience meaningful productivity gains, compared with 18.7% in advanced economies.
Complementing Human Labour: AI is more likely to support the work of many employees in developing countries than replace them, increasing their capabilities and efficiency.
Affordable, Task-Specific Tools: AI applications designed for specific tasks can make useful expertise more accessible to businesses, households and public institutions.
Improving Public Service Delivery: AI can assist teachers, support medical diagnosis, improve agricultural advice and strengthen public administration, expanding access to essential services.
Strength in Technology Deployment: India’s experience in deploying technology at population scale provides a strong foundation for applying AI to practical development challenges.
Agricultural Productivity: In Baramati, AI-supported farming reportedly increased sugarcane yields by 40% while reducing water and fertiliser use by 30%, demonstrating the potential for resource-efficient agriculture.
Healthcare Screening: AI-based tuberculosis detection has reportedly increased detection by 35%, while Wadhwani AI’s screening tools demonstrate the potential to strengthen healthcare delivery.
Weather Forecasting: India combined multiple AI models to provide monsoon forecasts and farming advisories to millions through text, voice and AI-powered services, predicting the unusual 2025 monsoon.
Multilingual Farmer Services: Bharat VISTAAR and state-level AI chatbots can provide farmers with locally relevant information in multiple languages, improving access to agricultural advice.

sum.text:
Prime Minister Narendra Modi has completed 25 years in public service: 13 as Gujarat’s chief minister and 12 as India’s Prime Minister. It is time to recall his major achievements and the challenges the nation faces over the next 10 years or so. Given my limitations as an agricultural economist, I will restrict my piece to agriculture’s performance in Gujarat and at the all-India level. I will also spell out what PM Modi still needs to do in agriculture to put it on a high and sustainable growth path that can significantly augment farmers’ incomes.
Let me start briefly with his term as Gujarat CM from 2001-02 to 2013-14. Gujarat agriculture experienced a miracle, registering growth of more than 9 per cent per annum. This was almost unheard of even in the heyday of the Green Revolution in Punjab. This achievement owed much to his strong emphasis on augmenting water supply for irrigation through check dams, as well as securing a good share of Narmada River waters. He also separated feeder lines for irrigation and rural households to ensure that power reached farmers on time for irrigation. Roads were given equally high priority, connecting farmers to markets. Extension work through Krishi Mahotsav brought together government functionaries and the private sector to reach farmers in every village and showcase the latest technologies. Bt cotton, approved by the Atal Bihari Vajpayee government in 2002, achieved wonders in Gujarat and created rural prosperity. These achievements also helped him become CM for four terms, until he became Prime Minister in 2014.
The year he took over as Prime Minister, India was hit by droughts in 2014 and 2015. Back-to-back droughts had occurred only three times in a century. His experience in Gujarat came in handy, and Modi accorded high priority to water (irrigation) along with crop insurance (PM Fasal Bima Yojana). As a result, almost 60 per cent of India’s gross cropped area is irrigated today. This has given India much-needed food security in basic staples. India has emerged as the largest producer and exporter of rice, and even after providing free food (rice or wheat, 5 kg per person per month) under the PM Garib Kalyan Yojana, we have buffer stocks that are more than four times the norm for rice and almost three times that for wheat.

explain.headline: UPSC Editorial Analysis: The Evolution of India’s Rural Employment Guarantee
static: MGNREGA 2005 was enacted under the mandate of Article 41 of the Constitution (Right to Work) to ensure at least 100 days of guaranteed wage employment.
The original framework operationalized Directive Principles of State Policy by providing a legally actionable right to public assistance in cases of unemployment.
Statutory penalties under the original act included the mandatory payment of unemployment allowances when work was not provided within 15 days of demand.
Traditional work under MGNREGA frequently drew criticism for generating non-durable assets such as kachha bunds washed away in rains.
explain.what: The transition from MGNREGA to VB-G RAM G introduces a 60-day operational pause, a 60:40 funding split, and digital authentication, sparking debates over rural welfare and federal fiscal burdens.
explain.why_in_news: Recent data from the Ministry of Rural Development showed a drop of 9.56 crore person-days generated during the July-August period compared to the previous year.
explain.background: MGNREGA 2005 provided a demand-driven legal entitlement of 100 days of unskilled manual work funded entirely by the Centre, operationalizing Article 41 of the Constitution.
significance: Highlights the ongoing tension between fiscal federalism, state matching grants, and central welfare mandates.
Examines how technological authentication affects digital exclusion among rural manual labourers.
Assesses the shift from a rights-based entitlement model to an administratively rationed mission framework.
prelims: Ministry of Rural Development data showed a drop of 9.56 crore person-days during the July-August period.
The funding architecture under VB-G RAM G uses a 60:40 Centre-State sharing pattern.
The revamped framework targets expanding employment from 100 to 125 days per household.
The restructured scheme introduces a mandatory 60-day operational pause during peak agricultural seasons.

Introduction The transition from the Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act (MGNREGA), 2005, to the revamped Viksit Bharat-Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission Gramin (VB-G RAM G) marks a significant shift in India’s rural …

points: The transition from MGNREGA 2005 to the revamped Viksit Bharat-Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission Gramin (VB-G RAM G) marks a significant shift in rural policy.
Recent Ministry of Rural Development data shows a drop of 9.56 crore person-days generated during the July-August period compared to the previous year.
This trend has ignited a major policy debate within Indian governance, macroeconomic management, and federal relations.
The restructured scheme introduces a mandatory 60-day operational pause during peak agricultural sowing and harvesting seasons.
The funding architecture shifted from the Union Government bearing 100% of unskilled wage costs to a 60:40 Centre-State sharing pattern.
Mandatory digital architecture includes app-based real-time attendance, facial recognition technology, and Aadhaar-based KYC protocols.
The revamped framework formally set an ambitious target of expanding guaranteed employment from 100 to 125 days per household.
Critics argue the 60-day pause removes the automatic safety net and technological hurdles cause genuine labourers to be turned away.
Poorer states struggle to mobilize their 40% matching contribution on time, creating funding choke points and delaying wage disbursements.
sum.text:
General Studies-2; Topic: Government policies and interventions for development in various sectors and issues arising out of their design and implementation.
The transition from the Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act (MGNREGA), 2005, to the revamped Viksit Bharat-Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission Gramin (VB-G RAM G) marks a significant shift in India’s rural policy framework.
Recent data from the Ministry of Rural Development indicates a drop of 9.56 crore person-days generated during the July–August period compared to the previous year (falling from 29.77 crore to 20.21 crore).
This trend has ignited a major policy debate within Indian governance, macroeconomic management, and federal relations.
Historical Foundation: Enacted in 2005 under the mandate of Article 41 of the Constitution (Right to Work), MGNREGA created an enforceable legal entitlement ensuring at least 100 days of guaranteed wage employment per financial year for rural households willing to do unskilled manual work.

The Indian Himalayan Region (IHR) is facing increasingly frequent and severe climate-induced disasters as temperatures rise, glaciers retreat and mountain slopes become unstable. Warming in Asia’s high mountains is occurring at 0.3°C per decade, nearly twice the global average. These changes threaten lives, infrastructure, water security and livelihoods, while exposing the limits of development that fails to account for Himalayan ecological and geological conditions across the region.
Rapid Glacier Loss: Ice-loss rates across the Hindu Kush Himalaya (HKH) have doubled since 2000, while Himalayan glaciers are losing mass 65% faster than a decade ago, increasing regional instability.
Uneven Warming Patterns: The western Himalaya is warming faster than the central and eastern stretches, with night-time minimum and winter temperatures rising at particularly high rates.
Limited Scientific Understanding: Only about 21 of the estimated 40,000 glaciers across the Himalaya-Karakoram region receive detailed, sustained monitoring, leaving major gaps in understanding changing mountain conditions.
Growing Disaster Concentration: Although the Himalayas cover around 18% of Indian land, they account for approximately 35% of disasters, showing the region’s disproportionate exposure to hazards.
A Shared Natural System: The Himalayas form part of the global mountain system extending from the Hindu Kush and Karakoram, and their ecological instability threatens communities across national borders.
Rising Temperatures Accelerate Melting: Higher atmospheric temperatures disturb the balance between winter snow accumulation and summer melting. Ice that once had temperatures of −6°C to −20°C is now closer to −2°C, making it more susceptible to melting.
Meltwater Weakens Glaciers: Meltwater enters deep shafts called moulins and reaches the bedrock, forming a pressurised layer between the rock and ice. This layer accelerates glacier movement, while water channels within and beneath the ice generate forces that can fracture it.
Permafrost Thaw Destabilises Slopes: Permafrost acts as geological cement by filling rock fractures with ice, but rising temperatures weaken this natural support and trigger rock avalanches, landslides and debris flows.
Glacial Lake Instability Increases Flood Risks: Retreating glaciers leave expanding lakes behind unstable deposits of rock and ice, increasing the possibility of sudden floods when their natural barriers fail.

The strategic shift culminated in high-level visits by PM Narendra Modi to Moscow and Kyiv, followed by backchannel diplomacy by S Jaishankar and Ajit Doval.

sum.text:
Since the outbreak of the Russia-Ukraine war, global diplomacy has fractured along predictable geopolitical fault lines. However, India's positioning has undergone a remarkable evolution. Originally taking a cautious, neutral stance characterised by its declaration that "Europe's problems are not the world's problems", New Delhi has steadily transitioned into an active diplomatic intermediary.
By putting forward a tangible, phased peace roadmap, India has emerged as a rare, credible bridge between Moscow and Kyiv, leveraging its unique diplomatic equity to de-escalate the conflict. For the first few years of the conflict, India’s approach was defined by rhetorical commitments to peace, balanced against its strategic dependencies. New Delhi maintained strong, historically deep ties with Moscow—resisting Western pressure and continuing to purchase discounted Russian energy—while simultaneously engaging with the West and offering humanitarian aid to Ukraine.
Prime Minister (PM) Narendra Modi famously encapsulated this early philosophy by telling Russian President Vladimir Putin that "today’s era is not an era of war." However, India’s strategy evolved from passive neutrality into active conflict resolution. This transition culminated in high-level shuffles, including PM Modi's visits to both Moscow and Kyiv, alongside intensive diplomatic follow-ups by external affairs minister S Jaishankar and National Security Adviser Ajit Doval. India moved decisively beyond simply advocating for peace, stepping forward to conduct practical, backchannel discussions on reducing hostilities.
India’s current peace push is anchored in a concrete, three-part ceasefire plan. Rather than immediately attempting to untangle the deeply intractable political questions of territorial sovereignty or NATO security guarantees, New Delhi’s strategy targets "second-order" agreements. The plan focuses on immediate, shared economic and humanitarian pain points that have global ramifications.

sum.text:
THE Supreme Court’s intervention in the ongoing protests in Delhi drives home the vital point that maintaining law and order cannot come at the cost of constitutional freedom. By directing the authorities to prevent illegal detention, restore normal metro services and ensure uninterrupted Internet access, subject to law, the Court has reaffirmed a fundamental principle of democracy: peaceful dissent is a right, not a privilege granted by the government. The protests organised by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) and some student organisations against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar have triggered an extraordinary security response.
The detention of more than 7,000 people on Saturday and hundreds of them on Sunday raises serious questions about the proportionality of the police action. Reports of barricaded roads, restricted Metro stations and alleged mistreatment of protesters add to concerns about the limits of preventive policing. The authorities are undoubtedly responsible for protecting public safety.
They have the right to act against violence, obstruction and credible threats to public order. However, such powers must be exercised within the bounds of the law. Detaining people merely for assembling peacefully, restricting movement far beyond designated prohibitory zones or disrupting essential public services — doesn’t it all amount to punishing hapless citizens?
Notably, the Court has issued directions to remove prohibitory notices around its premises so that citizens and lawyers can approach the apex institution without fear or obstruction. The allegations of unlawful detention and excessive force must be investigated impartially. The police, too, deserve a fair hearing.
Accountability should apply equally to protesters and law enforcement agencies. Public confidence in democratic institutions depends on credible answers, open scrutiny and institutional independence. A strong democracy does not fear peaceful protesters.
It addresses their grievances, protects public order without suppressing dissent and respects judicial directions. The Court has drawn an important line. The government must now try to ensure that constitutionally guaranteed freedom is not crushed on the streets of the Capital.
That won’t be an easy task, considering that the CJP and the Opposition remain defiant.

points: Indian economic discourse is trapped in an exhausting loop focusing excessively on headline GDP growth figures to the first decimal point.
Goodhart's Law dictates that when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure of actual national progress.
China's development shows world-class infrastructure and a biological marker of holistic progress: teenagers are significantly taller than their parents.
Data from The Lancet shows the average 19-year-old Chinese male stands at 5 ft 9 in, a gain of nearly 4 inches over 55-year-old men.
Height increases cannot be manufactured like GDP; they require decades of rising household incomes, better nutrition, and reliable healthcare.
While India's extreme poverty rate roughly halved in the past decade from over 20 percent to about 12 percent, development gaps remain.
India's childhood stunting rate for children under 5 remains over 35 percent, which is nearly seven times that of China.
GDP should be treated merely as a fuel and a compass rather than mistaking the map for the territory of human development.
sum.text: The Indian economic discourse has recently found itself trapped in a familiar, exhausting loop. With every release of GDP figures, a predictable tug-of-war ensues. On one side, we see celebration of 'fastest-growing major economy' status. On the other, multiple commentators question deflator methodologies, base year revisions, and the gap with observable ground realities. Our collective obsession with a single headline number - GDP growth to the first decimal point - may be the problem. One is reminded of Goodhart's Law: when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure. GDP is a vital barometer. But it's a blunt, singular instrument. It may tell you how fast the wheels are turning. But it doesn't always tell you if the vehicle is reaching its destination. To truly understand a nation's trajectory, one must adopt a more holistic view of development. China's GDP figures have been a subject of intense global scepticism for years. Yet, on the ground, the debate over whether the growth was 5% or 6% feels secondary to the undeniable reality of the development that has taken place. Infrastructure is no longer about 'potential' but a finished, world-class reality. From futuristic airports to a bullet train network to preponderance of EVs, the scale is unmatched. But development is never a straight line. China's real estate crisis is not just a headline but a visible landscape. Massive residential projects that once padded GDP figures now stand mothballed or abandoned - reminders that when a single metric (like GDP-contributing construction) becomes the sole target, the result can be a profound misallocation of capital. But the most striking observation of anyone visiting China has nothing to do with infrastructure or innovation. It's a biological manifestation of holistic progress: teenagers. Walking through Shanghai or Hefei, one is struck by teenagers being significantly taller than their parents. This anecdotal observation is confirmed from data from The Lancet that the average male 19-yr-old Chinese now stands at 5 ft 9 in. This represents a staggering gain of nearly 4 in (10 cm) over the height of the average 55-yr-old Chinese man. Chinese youth have now achieved height parity with their counterparts in the US and Britain. This observation isn't an argument to replace GDP with a 'tape measure' as our primary economic tool. Rather, it serves as a powerful proxy for the totality of development. You can manufacture GDP by building 'ghost cities',…

Ahead of the mid-term polls in the US, President Donald Trump has inked a deal with Russia wherein the latter will immediately supply 300,000 tonnes of diesel to the “American and global marketplace”, with 500,000 tonnes in November, followed by a million after that. Trump has also stated that the delivery is dependent on the functioning of Russian refineries currently under attack by Ukraine. Major amendments in 2004, 2008, 2012, and 2019 progressively expanded its scope to include economic security threats and individual terrorist designations.
Section 13 covers unlawful activities while Section 15 defines terrorist acts intended to threaten the unity or economic security of India.
The Act empowers the Central Government to declare associations unlawful and designate both organizations and individuals as terrorists.

sum.text:
The Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act (UAPA), 1967 is India’s primary anti-terror and national security law. While it plays a crucial role in safeguarding national security and territorial integrity, its stringent provisions have raised concerns regarding civil liberties, personal freedom and the potential for misuse.
The Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act (UAPA), 1967 is an anti-terrorism law enacted to prevent unlawful activities and protect the sovereignty, unity and integrity of India.
It empowers the government to declare associations unlawful, designate individuals as terrorists, and take strict action against terrorist activities.
1967 Origin: Enacted to ban “ unlawful associations ” and prevent secessionist movements threatening India’s integrity.
2004 Amendment: Incorporated core anti-terror provisions into the UAPA following the repeal of the Prevention of Terrorism Act (POTA).
2008 & 2012 Amendments: Expanded the definition of “ terrorist acts ” (including threats to economic security/counterfeiting) and strengthened investigative powers following the 2008 Mumbai attacks.
2019 Amendment: Granted the government the power to designate individuals as terrorists (previously restricted to organizations) and empowered the National Investigation Agency (NIA) to seize property linked to terrorism without state police permission.
Unlawful Activity (Section 13): Refers to actions that support or incite the cession or secession of any part of India, or disclaim/question India’s sovereignty and territorial integrity.
Terrorist Act (Section 15): Includes acts intended to threaten the unity, integrity, security, economic security (e.g. smuggling high-quality counterfeit currency), or sovereignty of India, or to strike terror in people.
Declaration of Unlawful Associations : Empowers the Central Government to declare an association unlawful if it engages in activities prejudicial to India’s sovereignty, unity and integrity.
Designation of Terrorists : Under Section 35, the Central Government can designate organisations and individuals as terrorists.
Punishment for Terrorist Activities : Provides strict penalties for terrorist acts, including imprisonment and the death penalty in certain cases.
Prohibition of Terrorist Organisations : Provides for the listing of terrorist organisations and restrictions on their activities and support.

points: Delhi Police withdrew Jantar Mantar's status as a designated protest site through an order issued on October 11 by Police Commissioner Anurag Kumar.
Three alternative venues were designated: Ramlila Maidan, CBD Ground in East Delhi, and Burari Ground in North Delhi.
The decision follows recent agitations that disrupted traffic and functioning in the New Delhi district, which houses Parliament and key government offices.
The Union Ministry of Home Affairs had constituted a committee to examine suitable alternatives, leading to the modifications of an earlier April 2022 standing order.
The three new sites are located at varying distances from Jantar Mantar: Ramlila Maidan is 4 km away, CBD Ground is 12 to 13 km away, and Burari Ground is 21 km away.
The move comes amid heightened security and calls for protests by the Cockroach Janta Party and opposition leaders, following recent confrontations like the July 20 clashes.
Opposition leaders including Jairam Ramesh and Akhilesh Yadav criticized the move as an assault on democracy and a sign of panic, while organizers like Saurav Das rejected it.
The Delhi High Court agreed to hear a petition concerning the closure, with petitioners arguing that peaceful demonstrations are being curtailed.
sum.text:
New Delhi: Delhi Police has withdrawn Jantar Mantar’s status as a designated protest site and named Ramlila Maidan, Burari Ground and CBD Ground in East Delhi as alternative venues for demonstrations, a decision that has drawn criticism from opposition parties and protest organisers and is facing legal scrutiny. The order, issued by Police Commissioner Anurag Kumar on October 11, follows a series of agitations in recent months that disrupted traffic and the functioning of New Delhi district, which houses Parliament, key government offices and the residences of senior constitutional authorities. The move marks a significant change for a venue that has served for decades as a gathering point for citizens seeking to bring their grievances directly to the attention of those in power.
According to the standing order, the Union Ministry of Home Affairs had constituted a committee to examine suitable alternatives that would allow citizens to organise protests and demonstrations. Acting on the committee’s recommendations, the police denotified Jantar Mantar and designated three new locations. The order modifies an earlier standing order dated April 28, 2022.
Detailed and revised standard operating procedures for conducting demonstrations at the new venues will be issued separately. The three sites are located at varying distances from the existing protest venue. Ramlila Maidan in Central Delhi is about four kilometres from Jantar Mantar, CBD Ground in East Delhi is around 12 to 13 kilometres away, and Burari Ground in North Delhi is nearly 21 kilometres away.
The decision comes amid heightened security arrangements in the capital after calls for protests at Jantar Mantar by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) and opposition leaders. The developments have also reached the courts. The Delhi High Court agreed on Monday to hear on Tuesday a petition concerning the closure of Jantar Mantar as a protest venue.
A lawyer told a bench of Acting Chief Justice Nitin Wasudeo Sambre and Justice Sanjay Sharma that peaceful demonstrations were being curtailed because authorities had not provided an alternative site. The bench noted that the Supreme Court was also examining the issue and had asked the Union government to file affidavits. Political reactions to the police order were sharply divided from the government’s position.
Congress general secretary in charge of communications Jairam Ramesh accused Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Union Home Minister Amit Shah of being afraid…

The Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs (CCEA), chaired by Prime Minister Narendra Modi, on Wednesday approved the continuation and integration of two key food distribution schemes under a new umbrella programme titled “Scheme for Assistance in Ration Transport and Handling-Income with Automation in PDS” (SARTHAK-PDS).
The Centre will spend ₹25,530 crore over the next five years as its share for the implementation of the scheme during the 16th Finance Commission cycle, with the programme set to continue until March 31, 2031.
The SARTHAK-PDS scheme integrates two existing initiatives – “Assistance to State Agencies for intra-State movement of foodgrains and FPS dealers’ margin under NFSA” and the “Scheme for Modernization and Reforms through Technology in Public Distribution System (SMART PDS)” – with the objective of strengthening implementation of the National Food Security Act.
The scheme is aimed at ensuring assured financial support for intra-state transportation and handling of foodgrains, along with enhanced margins for Fair Price Shop (FPS) dealers to improve last-mile delivery under the Public Distribution System (PDS).
The Cabinet has also approved revised norms for Central assistance to states and Union Territories to meet expenditure related to intra-state movement and handling of foodgrains and FPS dealer margins, while retaining the existing funding pattern.
The government said the integrated scheme seeks to build a unified, citizen-centric and technology-driven PDS architecture to minimise leakages, improve transparency and strengthen food security for beneficiaries covered under the NFSA.
The scheme proposes the use of advanced technologies such as Artificial Intelligence (AI), Machine Learning (ML), Natural Language Processing (NLP) and Blockchain to modernise and optimise PDS operations.
The government said the initiative would enable the creation of standardised digital architectures and unified databases for real-time monitoring, AI-driven grievance redressal and analytics systems, state-level command and control centres, and ISO-certified process frameworks to improve transparency, security and sustainability in PDS operations.
The government said the programme would support its commitment to ensuring food and nutritional security for around 81.35 crore beneficiaries covered under the NFSA.

sum.text:
India’s expanding network of free trade agreements (FTAs) could add around $140 billion to its gross domestic product (GDP) by 2035 and increase exports by 6.2%, according to a report by Bloomberg Economics.
The report said the agreements could help India access new markets, lower import costs, attract foreign direct investment (FDI) and improve productivity as countries increasingly diversify supply chains and seek preferential access to overseas markets.
“Using a large-scale model of the global economy developed by the World Trade Organisation, we estimate these agreements could add about $140 billion to India’s GDP in 2035, opening new markets, cutting import costs, fostering foreign direct investment and lifting productivity,” said the Bloomberg report.
“We also consider two scenarios that could amplify the gains: realising further productivity benefits from a decade of reforms to strengthen manufacturing competitiveness, and enacting policies that help underemployed agricultural workers transition into manufacturing and services,” the report added.
The expansion of India’s trade network comes as rising US tariffs reshape global trade flows. Since President Donald Trump returned to the White House in January 2025, the United States has increased tariffs on several trading partners and product categories.
According to Bloomberg Economics, the average US tariff rate stood at 10.7% in August, compared with 2.3% in 2024. The increase reflected sector-specific duties, particularly on automobiles and metals, as well as country-specific levies.
The report said tariffs at these levels could reduce US imports of goods by around 15% compared with the previous regime. Further increases remain possible amid continuing tariff threats and investigations.
In response, economies are seeking to diversify their trade relationships and accelerate negotiations with new partners, creating opportunities for countries that can secure preferential market access.
India has accelerated its FTA programme after years of relative caution. During 2025-26, agreements with the European Free Trade Association (EFTA), the United Kingdom and Oman entered into force, adding to trade agreements with Australia and the United Arab Emirates that took effect in 2022.

sum.text:
The Supreme Court was on Monday urged to urgently list contempt petitions alleging violation of its 2024 judgment on genetically modified crops, amid concerns over the alleged approval for the cultivation of herbicide-tolerant GM basmati rice. Lawyer Prashant Bhushan made the request before a bench comprising Chief Justice Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana. He said the contempt pleas should be heard at the earliest as approval had now been given for cultivating herbicide-tolerant GM basmati rice, and argued that the petitions were separate from the pending reference on GM mustard.
Bhushan referred to the 2024 judgment delivered by a bench of Justices B V Nagarathna and Sanjay Karol, which gave a split verdict on one issue and referred it to a larger bench. He said the contempt petitions arose from the common judgment and were not connected to the reference listed before a special three-judge bench. “The contempt petitions are not related to the reference.
They arise out of the common judgment of the court. They can be listed before the regular contempt bench,” Bhushan submitted. He told the court that the contempt petition, filed in 2025, had not been taken up despite being mentioned earlier.
According to him, the special bench hearing the GM mustard reference had declined to hear the contempt petitions. “They have now given the go-ahead to plant genetically modified basmati rice, which is a herbicide-tolerant variety. It will contaminate and cause havoc,” Bhushan said while urging the court to list the matter urgently.
The contempt plea was filed by activist Aruna Rodrigues as part of her PIL initiated in 2025. It seeks contempt proceedings against senior government officials, alleging wilful and deliberate disobedience of the Supreme Court’s orders on the release of genetically modified and gene-edited crops. The petition alleged that the Centre violated the apex court’s July 23, 2024 judgment, which directed it to frame a comprehensive national policy on GM crops through a consultative process involving experts, state governments and other stakeholders before such crops were released.
It also alleged that herbicide-tolerant basmati rice varieties sold under the brand name RobiNOweed were commercially released in May 2024, while gene-edited rice varieties, including DRR Rice 100, sold as Kamla, and Pusa DST Rice 1, were released in May 2025. The decision came on a public interest litigation filed by Mahendra Kumar Mitra challenging the Karnataka Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes Reservation Act of 2022.
The core issue involved the state increasing total reservation from 50 percent to 56 percent, breaching the established 50 percent ceiling.
A bench of Chief Justice Vibhu Bakhru and Justice K.S. Hemalekha passed the order declaring the enhanced quota unconstitutional.
The revision was originally initiated by the then BJP government led by Basavaraj Bommai based on the Justice Nagamohan Das Committee recommendations.
The policy change increased SC reservation from 15 percent to 17 percent and ST reservation from 3 percent to 7 percent.

sum.text:
Bengaluru: In a significant setback to Karnataka's reservation policy, the High Court has quashed the state's decision to raise the reservation quota for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes to 17 per cent and 7 per cent, respectively. A bench comprising Chief Justice Vibhu Bakhru and Justice K.S. Hemalekha passed the order while considering a public interest litigation filed by Mahendra Kumar Mitra. The petitioner had challenged the law providing enhanced reservation in educational institutions and state government services under the Karnataka Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Reservation) Act, 2022.
The government's decision had increased the combined reservation for SCs and STs from 18 per cent to 24 per cent, taking the state's overall reservation percentage from 50 per cent to 56 per cent. The High Court has now struck down the measure that enabled the increase. Before the revision, Scheduled Castes were entitled to a 15 per cent reservation and Scheduled Tribes to 3 per cent.
The Justice Nagamohan Das Committee, constituted to examine the issue, recommended increasing the SC share to 17 per cent and the ST share to 7 per cent, citing population-based considerations. The recommendations received political backing at an all-party meeting, following which the then BJP government under Basavaraj Bommai initiated steps to implement the proposed changes. The state Cabinet approved a draft measure aimed at enhancing reservation for the Scheduled Communities.
The government subsequently promulgated an ordinance, which received the Governor's assent. A special gazette notification was later issued to formalise the revised quotas. Under the new arrangement, the SC reservation was increased by two percentage points, while the ST quota was raised by four percentage points.
The changes applied to 103 sub-castes categorised under the Scheduled Castes and 56 sub-groups recognised under the Scheduled Tribes. The increase was intended to revise the representation of the two communities in educational institutions and government employment. However, the legislation faced a legal challenge over the decision to increase the total reservation beyond the existing 50% level.
The petitioner approached the High Court questioning the validity of the enhanced reservation framework. After hearing the public interest litigation, the division bench ordered the cancellation of the government's decision to raise the overall quota to 56%. The judgment places Karnataka's…

Speaking during his visit to Mizoram, Scindia accused the Congress of possessing a double standard, accepting electoral outcomes when victorious, yet questioning democratic institutions, the Election Commission, and the judiciary whenever defeated.
Scindia highlighted the vast, multi-tiered nature of Indian democracy, stretching from national elections to grassroots Panchayat governance. He asserted that casting systematic doubts on election processes undermines public faith in the world's largest democratic mechanism.
"The protest staged by the Opposition in Delhi today is an affront to the democratic system. In a country where elections are held constantly, ranging from Lok Sabha and Assembly elections down to local body polls for Zila Panchayats and Sarpanchs, casting doubt or a slur upon that very system serves as yet another example of the Congress party’s true intent," he said.
Delhi protest LIVE: Congress Punjab in-charge Sachin Pilot on Monday joined the INDIA bloc’s protest march in the national capital, launching a blistering attack on the Election Commission of India (ECI) and the central government over alleged electoral fraud. We have provided proof of vote theft, which establishes that we must fight to save democracy."
Pilot emphasized that the controversy surrounding Gyanesh Kumar has cast a shadow of doubt over the fairness of India’s electoral system.
"The country is facing a major moral crisis. Elections in our country have always been fair, transparent, and impartial. This hasn't just started happening now; ever since Gyanesh Kumar rigged the votes, a doubt has been created in people's minds. Today, it’s not just about the Congress party; every young person and every true Indian citizen wants our elections to be protected. explain.headline: Global Multidimensional Poverty Rises for First Time Since 2010 Creation
static: The Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI) was developed in 2010 by the Oxford Poverty and Human Development Initiative (OPHI) and the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP).
It complements traditional monetary poverty measures by capturing the overlapping deprivations that poor people experience simultaneously in their daily lives.
The MPI assesses poverty across three core dimensions: health, education, and standard of living, using ten specific indicators.

The United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) is the UN's global development network, advocating for change and connecting countries to knowledge, experience, and resources to help build a better life.
OPHI is an economic research center based at the University of Oxford focused on multidimensional poverty measurement and reduction.

explain.background: The global Multidimensional Poverty Index measures acute deprivations across health, education, and living standards, serving as a key benchmark for international development progress.
significance: Highlights the compounding threats of population growth and data gaps on global poverty reduction targets.
Provides critical insights into child poverty, revealing that minors make up over half of those in acute poverty.
Offers a comparative evaluation of developing countries, tracking successful policy interventions in regions like Asia and sub-Saharan Africa.
prelims: The global poverty index rose for the first time since 2010.

explain.mains: Examine the factors contributing to the recent rise in global multidimensional poverty as highlighted by the UNDP, and discuss policy measures needed to reverse this trend.

points: The UN global poverty index has risen for the first time since 2010, affecting 1.2 billion people globally.
The 2026 report by UNDP and Oxford Poverty and Human Development Initiative found 51.5 million more people in acute poverty.
UNDP Administrator Alexander De Croo called the increase a wake-up call highlighting interlocking hardships like hunger and lack of clean water.
More than half of the individuals suffering from acute poverty globally were children.
A major driver of the recorded increase was population growth combined with new data being available for only 13 of 108 developing countries.
Despite the rise, 33 nations halved their percentage of people living in poverty over the past 15 years.
Rapid progress was recorded in Asian nations like China and Vietnam, along with reductions in Egypt, Nepal, and Tajikistan.
The majority of the poorest populations continue to reside in sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia.
The poverty index assesses indicators such as inadequate housing, sanitation, electricity, cooking fuel, food, and education.
sum.text:
WASHINGTON: A UN global poverty index has risen for the first time since its creation in 2010, bringing the number of people affected to 1.2 billion, the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) reported Monday.
In the 2026 edition of their annual report, the UNDP and the Oxford Poverty and Human Development Initiative research center counted 51.5 million more people living in "acute" poverty compared to the previous year.
UNDP Administrator Alexander De Croo said the increase in poverty should be a "wake-up call for the world."
"Behind these figures are 1.2 billion people facing hardships that reinforce one another: hunger, missed schooling and a lack of clean water or electricity. This is unacceptable," he said in a press release.
More than half of those in acute poverty were children.
However, UNDP said a major factor in the recorded increase was population growth, and new data was only available for 13 of the 108 developing countries covered by the report.
While the total number of people in poverty has increased, the report provides a mixed picture. Some 33 nations have halved the percentage of their people living in poverty as defined by the index in the past 15 years.
Those included six countries in sub-Saharan Africa. Among the countries that have made the most rapid progress were countries in Asia -- China and Vietnam -- UNDP said.
As in the previous year, the report found that the majority of the poorest people live in sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia, specifically the Indian subcontinent, the most densely populated region on Earth.
"In Egypt, Nepal, and Tajikistan, both the poverty rate and the number of people experiencing multidimensional poverty have decreased significantly," the press release said.
In Angola and Zambia, the poverty rate has also declined, but population growth has more than offset this decrease, resulting in an increase in the number of people living in poverty.
The poverty index used in the report includes indicators such as the lack of adequate housing, sanitation, electricity, cooking fuel, food and education.

He delivered the address at the 33rd Foundation Day celebrations of the National Human Rights Commission in New Delhi.
The core issue addressed was ensuring substantive access to safe drinking water and clarifying the distinct roles of courts and human rights institutions.
He acknowledged India's expansion of rural household tap connections but questioned whether delivered water is safe, reliable, and available when needed.
He highlighted that constitutional courts hold strong writ jurisdictions under Articles 32 and 226 to enforce remedies for rights infringements.
The CJI stressed that human rights commissions provide indispensable independent fact-finding machinery to identify systemic failures and assist marginalized communities.

sum.text:
Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant on Monday underscored that constitutional courts must intervene whenever fundamental freedoms are violated..CJI Kant made the observation while speaking at the National Human Rights Commission's (NHRC) Foundation Day celebrations. In his address, the CJI noted that the NHRC has decided to mark the event with a conference on water. "India itself has made astronomical efforts to expand access to drinking water, including through the provision of household tap connections in rural areas.
That progress deserves commendation. But the next question must be a more demanding one: Is the water safe, reliable and available when the family needs it?" he remarked. He went on to comment on the importance of ensuring access to clean water, and the role of courts and human rights watchdogs in enforcing such rights." A mere tap is not the same as access to water … Government must build and maintain the systems through which water reaches people.
Courts must intervene when constitutional rights are violated. Human Rights Commissions must investigate complaints, identify systemic failures and ensure that concerns which may otherwise remain invisible receive institutional attention," he said. The CJI also spoke extensively on the vital role played by human rights commissions.
The Chief Justice noted that while constitutional courts exercise robust writ jurisdictions under Articles 32 and 226 of the Constitution of India to enforce remedies, human rights commissions possess vital fact-finding machinery.“People sometimes say that the Commission can only recommend and cannot command. But I would offer an alternative perspective … Its purpose is not to still the waves of injustice, but to cast a guiding light for those adrift in the darkness … The influence of a human rights institution does not come from the coercive force of its orders, but from the credibility it earns over time." he said. These commissions, he observed, are uniquely equipped to initiate independent inquiries, assess administrative deficiencies on the ground, and elevate grievances of marginalised communities who often lack the resources to access formal litigation..The CJI was speaking at the 33rd Foundation Day celebrations of the NHRC at Vigyan Bhavan, New Delhi.

sum.text:
The Allahabad high court has called on the law commission to consider recommending changes to the protection of children from sexual offences (POCSO) Act, 2012, to address cases involving minor couples while taking India's prevailing social realities into account. A two-judge bench comprising justice Atul Sreedharan and Justice Achal Sachdev said that the strict enforcement of the legislation could, in certain exceptional circumstances, lead to outcomes that “advance injustice rather than justice”, especially when a relationship has resulted in the birth of a child. The comment was made during the court's consideration of Rakesh Yadav's habeas corpus petition, which sought an order to produce his wife.
The bench observed that the law appeared not to have adequately considered India's social conditions, where a substantial section of the population remains illiterate or semi-literate and may have limited awareness of their legal and constitutional rights, along with the responsibilities and consequences associated with them. The girl's father told the court that she had studied up to class 5 but could not read a newspaper and was able only to sign her name. He said he had never attended school.
The court allowed the man's habeas corpus petition. The couple had eloped, and the girl subsequently gave birth to their child, following which a case was registered against him under the POCSO Act. Court calls for flexibility in exceptional cases"It is definitely not an excuse to be ignorant of the law.
The bench noted that the POCSO Act's execution may, in some factual circumstances, lead to outcomes that seem to promote injustice rather than justice if this concept is implemented in a purely pedantic manner." According to the news agency PTI, the court suggested that the law commission consider amendments allowing special judges greater flexibility in exceptional cases to take the specific circumstances into account while deciding an appropriate sentence. It also recommended examining alternative penalties, including community service, in situations where applying the POCSO Act could lead to the unnecessary disruption of a family formed amid a lack of awareness of the law. The bench observed that the existing legislation appeared to have insufficiently considered India's prevailing social realities.

Context: The World Health Organization ( WHO ) has granted prequalification to CERVAVAC , making it the first Indian-made quadrivalent human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccine to meet global standards for quality, safety, and efficacy.
India’s first indigenously developed, gender-neutral quadrivalent Human Papillomavirus (qHPV) vaccine designed as a preventive oncology vaccine to protect against cervical cancer and HPV-related diseases.
Developed by: Manufactured and developed indigenously by the Serum Institute of India (SII), Pune.
High-Risk Oncogenic Strains (Types 16 and 18): Responsible for over 70% to 80% of all cervical cancer cases globally.
Low-Risk Strains (Types 6 and 11): Responsible for causing approximately 90% of anogenital warts (condyloma acuminata).
First Indigenous Prequalified HPV Vaccine : Stands as the first Indian-manufactured quadrivalent HPV vaccine on the WHO List of Prequalified Vaccines, joining an international pool previously dominated by foreign manufacturers.
Broad Age & Gender-Neutral Indication: Licensed in India for administration to both girls and boys aged 9 to 26 years , enabling herd immunity and preventing male HPV burdens such as anal cancers and genital warts.
Affordable & Scalable Production: Engineered to be substantially more cost-effective than imported counterparts, leveraging SII’s mass-scale manufacturing to address global supply crunches .
Flexible Dosing Regimen: Compatible with WHO-recommended schedules, supporting both single-dose or two-dose regimens for the primary target group of adolescents aged 9 to 14 years.
Rigorous International Quality Benchmark : Validated through extensive clinical evaluations, batch testing, and manufacturing facility audits to meet the stringent safety and immunogenicity guidelines of the WHO.
Accelerates progress toward the WHO’s 90-70-90 target (vaccinating 90% of girls by age 15 by 2030), directly expanding the affordable vaccine supply for Gavi and UNICEF across low- and middle-income countries (LMICs).
Provides an indigenous, WHO-standard HPV vaccine, reducing import dependence and procurement costs while strengthening India’s immunisation programme.

sum.text:
On 12 October 2026, PM-SETU approved ₹440 crore to upgrade nine Government Industrial Training Institutes (ITIs) in the Surat and Visakhapatnam clusters. The partnership covers five ITIs in Surat, Gujarat, and four in Visakhapatnam, Andhra Pradesh. Shareholders’ Agreements were signed by the Directorate General of Training (DGT), the Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship (MSDE), the two State Governments and ArcelorMittal Nippon Steel India (AM/NS India).
Industrial Training Institutes provide vocational training in trades to prepare trainees for skilled employment. Their training includes practical instruction in workshops and laboratories. The DGT functions under the MSDE and is associated with the administration of vocational training programmes, including the Craftsmen Training Scheme. ITIs form part of India’s formal vocational training system.
The approved initiative groups the nine ITIs into the Surat and Visakhapatnam clusters. Dedicated Special Purpose Vehicles (SPVs) will manage the upgradation and operations of the clusters. AM/NS India will hold 51% equity in the SPVs, while the Government of India and the respective State Government will each hold 24.5%. These shares account for the entire equity in each SPV.
AM/NS India will implement the programme with the New Age Makers’ Institute of Technology (NAMTECH) as its academic and technical partner. The partnership includes support for curriculum reforms and faculty development. Planned changes include modernising training infrastructure, workshops and laboratories, introducing trades linked to industry requirements and emerging technologies, and revising curricula. The agreements involve the Central Government, the Governments of Gujarat and Andhra Pradesh, and a private-sector industry partner.

The Supreme Court on Monday clarified that it has approved nor disapproved the Election Commission of India's (ECI) revised Form 6 for voter registration..Form 6 is to be filled by people seeking to register as voters for the first time. It is being used by the Election Commission of India (ECI) during the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls in various States..A bench of Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana said that the revised Form 6 did not exist when the Bihar SIR matter was heard, and that the Court's observations of October 5 cannot be construed as either approval or disapproval. The Court had on October 5 said that it had not approved any modification to Form 6.
The bench today sought to clarify the same, stating that the issue itself had never come up before it and hence, there was no occasion of the Court approving or disapproving the modification." What was said was that when the Bihar SIR matter was before us, the new Form 6 was not there. That does not mean it was either approved or disapproved by the Supreme Court," Justice Bagchi said. .The Supreme Court's clarification came after it was argued by a petitioner that the ECI has represented the revised Form 6 as having the Supreme Court's approval.
The counsel for the petitioner sought to highlight the Court's remarks of October 5." On October 5, this Court had already declared that Form 6 was not approved by the Supreme Court of India. But the Election Commission has published that the altered Form 6 has been approved by the Supreme Court. Astana, Oct 12 (IANS) The ninth edition of the India-Kazakhstan joint military exercise Kazind 2026 concluded at Kazakhstan's Oskemen, reaffirming the defence partnership between the two nations.
The exercise enhanced interoperability, strengthened professional camaraderie and reaffirmed the defence partnership between India and Kazakhstan.
"The 9th edition of India-Kazakhstan Joint Military Exercise KAZIND 2026 concluded at Oskemen, Kazakhstan, with a 72-hour validation exercise showcasing operational readiness, tactical coordination and joint counter-terrorism capabilities," the Indian Army's Additional Directorate General of Public Information posted on X.
"The exercise enhanced interoperability, strengthened professional camaraderie and reaffirmed the enduring defence partnership between the two nations," it added.
On October 6, the Indian Army and the Armed Forces of Kazakhstan conducted combat drills under Kazind 2026 in Kazakhstan’s Oskemen, aimed at sharpening battlefield skills, enhancing interoperability and strengthening operational preparedness.
“Indian Army and the Armed Forces of Kazakhstan are undertaking joint training during Exercise Kazind 2026 at Oskemen, Kazakhstan. The troops carried out tactical navigation through the Akhmirovo Training Area, engaged targets during live-firing drills and executed combined combat exercises, sharpening battlefield skills, coordination and interoperability between the two forces,” the Indian Army's Additional Directorate General of Public Information posted on X.
The opening ceremony of the Kazind 2026 was conducted at Oskemen on September 29. The ceremony was presided over by Major General Zhenis Maralov, Chief of Regional Command East of the Armed Forces of Kazakhstan.
A 60-member Indian Armed Forces contingent mainly from a battalion of the GARHWAL RIFLES, along with troops from other arms and services, and personnel from the Indian Air Force participated in the exercise. The Kazakhstan Armed Forces included a contingent of matching strength, comprising primarily personnel from its Land Forces, according to the Ministry of Defence statement.
The exercise was aimed at enhancing interoperability and strengthening the joint capability of both forces to undertake Joint Counter-Terrorism operations in a sub-conventional environment under a United Nations mandate.

The presence of combat, transport, surveillance and air-to-air refuelling platforms enabled aircrew, mission planners and support personnel to gain insights into each other’s capabilities and enhance coordination for operating in an increasingly complex security environment.
The exercise also highlighted India’s growing role in international defence engagement, with participation from 32 observer nations reflecting wider interest in the country’s military capabilities and expanding aerospace and defence sector.
The IAF’s experience during Operation Sindoor added to the relevance of the exercise, underscoring the importance of precision, integrated planning, operational preparedness and credible deterrence in contemporary warfare.
The operation demonstrated the role of air power in achieving national security objectives in a complex threat environment, according to the Defence Ministry.

The Uttarakhand government held its first cabinet meeting in Haridwar on Monday, chaired by Chief Minister Pushkar Singh Dhami, and approved various proposals involving welfare schemes, administrative reforms and strengthening infrastructure. The state cabinet first approved the Uttarakhand Floodplain Zoning Rules, 2026, to regulate land use and development activities in flood-prone areas. Officials said these rules will establish detailed procedures, standards, and operational frameworks to effectively implement the provisions of the Uttarakhand Floodplain Zoning Act, 2012.
They said the objective is to safeguard lives, property, and critical infrastructure from potential flood damage while maintaining the natural flow of floodwaters. The cabinet also gave in-principle approval for the formation of a society for the development of the Shri Madan Mohan Malviya Prachya Shodh Sansthan at Rishikul in Haridwar. The objective is to promote Indian knowledge traditions, ancient sciences, culture, and modern research, officials said.
In the meeting, approval was also granted for amending Schedule-3 under Section 49 of the Uttarakhand Investment and Infrastructure (Development and Regulation) Act, 2023. Under this initiative, a provision has been made to allocate 92 per cent of the proceeds derived from the disinvestment and monetisation of assets – belonging to public agencies, local bodies, state public sector undertakings, and financially autonomous institutions – to the respective public agencies. This measure will facilitate better asset management and accelerate infrastructure development, an official statement said.
The Cabinet has decided to table the second Uttarakhand Jan Vishwas (Amendment) Bill, 2026 in the upcoming legislative assembly session to simplify business activities and promote 'Ease of Doing Business' in the state. The Cabinet also greenlit the convening of the third session of the fifth Uttarakhand Legislative Assembly for 2026. Chief Minister Pushkar Singh Dhami was authorised to determine the date and venue for the assembly session.

explain.headline: The gaps in the implementation of the Right to Information Act
static: The Right to Information Act was enacted in 2005 to empower citizens, promote transparency and accountability, and give effect to the freedom of speech under Article 19(1)(a).
Section 3 guarantees the right to information, Section 4 mandates proactive disclosures, and Section 7 sets a 30-day time limit for providing information.
Sections 12 and 15 provide for the constitution of the Central Information Commission and State Information Commissions respectively to handle appeals and complaints.
Section 20 of the RTI Act provides for statutory penalties against Public Information Officers in specified cases of non-compliance and delay.
The RTI Amendment Act of 2019 altered the framework by allowing the Central Government to fix the tenure and salaries of information commissioners through rules.

explain.why_in_news: The RTI Act recently completed 21 years of enactment, drawing attention to its persistent operational challenges and implementation gaps.
explain.background: Enacted in 2005, the RTI Act promotes governance transparency through proactive disclosures and statutory mechanisms, but faces structural, digital, and administrative bottlenecks.
significance: Highlights the ground realities and institutional weaknesses plaguing India's primary transparency legislation.
Underscores the impact of executive control over Information Commissions on administrative accountability.
Serves as crucial study material for governance, transparency, and civil services ethics.
prelims: The RTI Act was enacted in the year 2005.
Section 4 of the RTI Act requires public authorities to proactively disclose prescribed information.
The standard time limit for providing information under Section 7 is 30 days, while for life or liberty cases it is 48 hours.
The RTI Amendment Act was passed in the year 2019.

points: The Right to Information Act has completed 21 years, bringing attention to persistent gaps in proactive disclosure despite improvements in transparency audits.
The RTI Act was enacted to promote transparency, accountability and informed citizen participation in governance by empowering Indian citizens to access information.
Section 4 of the Act requires public authorities to maintain records and proactively disclose prescribed information to reduce individual applications.
Many departments fail to publish mandatory information regularly, leaving government websites with outdated, incomplete or inaccessible data.
Pendency of appeals and complaints causes severe delays in case disposal, which weakens the deterrent effect of penalties against non-compliant officials.
Vacancies, inadequate institutional capacity, staff shortages, and concerns regarding the independence of Information Commissions hinder effective functioning.
Information seekers and RTI activists face limited protection and fear of retaliation when raising questions about powerful individuals or institutions.
The RTI Amendment Act, 2019 empowered the Central Government to prescribe tenure, salaries, allowances and service conditions through rules.
The digital divide, poor record management, administrative resistance, and limited awareness further compound the challenges in RTI implementation.
sum.text:
The Right to Information (RTI) Act, 2005 , has completed 21 years, drawing attention to persistent gaps in proactive disclosure despite improvements in transparency audits and public access to information.
The RTI Act was enacted to promote transparency, accountability and informed citizen participation in governance.
It empowers Indian citizens to access information held by public authorities, subject to statutory exemptions.
It gives practical effect to the right to information as an integral part of the freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution, as recognised by the Supreme Court.
Section 3: Guarantees the right to information to Indian citizens, subject to the Act.
Section 4: Requires public authorities to maintain records and proactively disclose prescribed information.
Section 6: Specifies the procedure for filing RTI applications.
Section 7: Generally requires information to be provided within 30 days. Where a request concerns the life or liberty of a person, the time limit is 48 hours.
Section 8: Lists exemptions from disclosure, including certain information affecting national security and personal privacy.
Sections 12 and 15: Provide for the constitution of the Central Information Commission (CIC) and State Information Commissions, respectively.
Section 19: Provides for appeals against decisions concerning access to information.
Section 20: Provides for penalties against Public Information Officers (PIOs) in specified cases of non-compliance.
Section 4 is central to the RTI framework because it requires public authorities to disclose important information on their own initiative, reducing the need for citizens to file individual applications.
What Must Be Disclosed: Section 4(1)(b) specifies 17 categories of information , including: The organisation, functions and duties of public authorities. Powers and responsibilities of officers and employees. Decision-making procedures and applicable rules. Regulations, manuals, instructions and records used in administration. Directories of officers and employees and their remuneration. Budget allocations, expenditure and details of subsidy programmes. Information about concessions, permits and their beneficiaries. Details of information available electronically. Facilities available to citizens for obtaining information. Names and contact details of Public Information Officers.
The organisation, functions and duties of public authorities.
Regulations, manuals,…

PATNA: The Bihar cabinet on Monday approved a proposal to improve air connectivity. Under the plan, five new airports and nine heliports will be made operational across the state. The districts where new airports will be built include Kishanganj, Saran, Begusarai, Araria and Gopalganj.
Nine heliports will be built in Aurangabad, Banka, Jamui, Katihar, Khagaria, Nawada, Sheikhpura and Sitamarhi districts. The state government will bear 25 per cent of the total cost and spend Rs. 10 lakh per annum on publicity during the operation of flights. The government will ensure free-of-cost pick-up and drop facilities to nearby towns from airports and heliports.
In addition, the government will also provide relaxations in taxes and extend financial support to the agencies. This will help the government provide better air connectivity to towns and cities. The proposed airports and heliports will be built in PPP mode..The cabinet also approved the construction of a five-star hotel at Vaishali, the noted tourist destination.
The state tourism department has already amended its earlier resolution to accelerate the construction of the hotel. The project will work under the PPP mode. Earlier, it was decided to build the resort on five acres of land, but the area has been extended to 10 acres.
Besides, a tech park will be developed in the Gardanibagh locality of Patna, which will provide jobs to 5,000 people. Bihar Chief Minister Samrat Choudhary, in his post-cabinet address, said that Bihar would be made a hub of entrepreneurship, employment and innovation under the BJP-led NDA government in the state. “Bihar will also contribute to building a developed India by 2047,” he added.
Choudhary said that all possible efforts would be made to make Bihar a major centre of investment, employment and entrepreneurship. Highlighting the contribution of Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Choudhary said that Bihar had made significant progress under the leadership of PM Modi.“Modi ji’s commitment to ensuring that the benefits of development reach socially marginalised people serves as an inspiration for all of us,” he said. During his 25-year-long journey from CM of Gujarat to PM of the country, circumstances kept changing, but the idea of ‘nation first, citizen first’ did not change for the Prime Minister, Choudhary said, adding that solving people’s problems had been a priority for the PM.He thanked PM Modi for showing his keen interest in Bihar’s development.

sum.text:
Pilibhit: Efforts to secure Ramsar site status for the 22.2-km-long Sharda Sagar Dam have stalled after the irrigation department refused to provide technical details sought by district authorities for the nomination, citing concerns over dam safety, irrigation and local livelihoods. The dispute has coincided with objections from forest officials to the department’s auction of commercial fishing rights in the reservoir, part of which falls within the eco-sensitive zone of Pilibhit Tiger Reserve (PTR). The fishing activities are feared to create perilous conditions for survival of dam’s aquatic wildlife, especially turtle and crocodile protected under Schedule I of Wildlife (Protection) Act, apart from migratory birds.
The impasse followed directions issued earlier this year by the Uttar Pradesh chief secretary to the principal secretary of environment, forest and climate change and the district magistrates of Pilibhit and Balrampur to prepare Ramsar nomination proposals for Sharda Sagar Dam and Chittorgarh Reservoir, PTR divisional forest officer (DFO) Manish Singh said. Pilibhit DM Alok Kumar asked Sharda Sagar division executive engineer Praveen Prakash Gautam on June 4 to provide the required information to the PTR DFO. After receiving no response, he sent a reminder on Aug 18.
In his Aug 27 reply, Gautam declined to share the details, arguing that Ramsar designation could complicate emergency water drainage and repairs under the Dam Safety Act, 2021. He also raised concerns that maintaining water levels for ecological purposes could disrupt irrigation across more than 1.26 lakh hectares in Shahjahanpur, Unnao, Hardoi, Raebareli and Lucknow during three cropping seasons annually. Gautam further warned that potential restrictions on fishing, grass harvesting and lotus seed farming could affect local livelihoods, while curbs on maintenance activities could hamper dam operations.
Meanwhile, forest authorities objected to the irrigation department’s auction of commercial fishing rights in the reservoir, warning that fishing nets could trap protected aquatic species.“The auction of the dam’s water area for commercial fishing is illegal as crocodiles mainly prey on fish species. Secondly, the dam is home to around 11 Schedule I turtle species. Fishing nets will also trap turtles and crocodiles, posing a threat to their survival and population growth,” Singh said.
